items.title: 13.2 Trend in volatility of the halogens

blocks.text: Halogens are non-polar, so instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces play the main role in their volatility. These forces depend on molecular size, shape and polarisability: stronger forces mean lower volatility and higher boiling points. Substances with weak id-id forces, with smaller, less polarisable molecules, have lower boiling points and higher volatility; larger, more polarisable molecules with stronger London dispersion forces have higher boiling points and lower volatility. Volatility is inversely related to boiling point: a more volatile substance has a lower boiling point, because stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to separate the molecules from the liquid into the gas (Table 13.2).

blocks.caption: Effect of London forces on physical properties (Table 13.2)

blocks.text: The first two halogens, fluorine (colourless or very light green) and chlorine (greenish-yellow), are gases because of weaker id-id forces. Bromine is a liquid because its molecule is bigger and has stronger intermolecular forces than fluorine and chlorine; iodine has the strongest forces in the group, so it is a solid at room temperature.
